supplement.where: https://github.com/paul-rottger/ai-distortion (p. 16, Data and Code Availability Statement). The saved PDF ends with references on p. 20; it has no supplementary appendix or embedded attachment.
supplement.holds: The main paper refers to SI:1.4 for attrition; SI:2.3-2.4 for exact writer/reader questions; SI:5.1 and SI:8.3 for rating distributions; SI:5.2 and SI:5.6 for robustness/main regressions; SI:5.7-5.8 for model/input comparisons; SI:5.9 for SD/entropy homogenization analyses; SI:4.2, SI:7.3 and SI:8.5 for editing/preferences; SI:8.2 for reward-model evaluation; SI:8.4 for mitigation regressions; and SI:9.4 and SI:10.4 for trust/persuasion regressions (pp. 4, 11-15). These references establish where fuller results are said to be available; the actual supplement and its numerical SEs/CIs could not be inspected. GitHub API, raw GitHub, and the OSF preregistration API were inaccessible.

paper_design_summary: UK Prolific writers first composed political opinion paragraphs and then edited AI-generated alternatives; independent blinded readers rated originality, writing quality, and perceived writer characteristics in Studies 1 and 3. The main Study 1 AI-versus-unaided comparisons used a fixed order, whereas Study 3 randomized the order of three AI configurations within writers and supports core ai_design comparisons. Study 2 randomized disclaimers but collected no third-party output ratings; Studies 4 and 5 randomized reader exposure to existing paragraphs and measured trust or persuasion.

studies.label: Study 1: Main writing and persona-perception study

assignment.what_was_assigned: The recorded pooled AI-versus-unaided contrasts compare the same writers in a fixed human-first sequence; AI availability and its order were not randomized. Within that study, AI models and input formats were randomly paired across each writer, rewrite versus improve was randomized for paragraph input, and reader paragraph assignments were randomized (pp. 3, 12, Figure 1 and Sections 4.4, 4.6). Those configuration manipulations do not randomize the pooled contrast recorded here; their attribute-specific estimates are referred to SI:5.7-5.8.
assignment.quote: after writers had composed their own paragraph and edited the AI-generated version to their satisfaction
assignment.locator: p. 3, Figure 1 and Section 2; p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 12, Sections 4.4 and 4.6
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/6exf2 (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: Own paragraph (unaided reference)
arms.description: Writers first compose their own paragraph. Same writer sample as the AI condition; no independent no-AI group (p. 3, Figure 1). Arm-specific distinct writer counts after the analysis restriction are not stated.

arms.name: AI-assisted paragraph (including writer edits)
arms.description: AI drafts from stance, bullets, or the existing paragraph and the writer may edit it. Main comparison includes edits and excludes cases where AI text was strictly dispreferred (pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and Section 2.2).

participants.exclusions: Initial assignment and attrition counts are not supplied; attrition is referred to absent SI:1.4 (p. 11). The main perception analysis removes 708 of 4,503 writer-proposition cases (15.7%) where AI text was strictly dispreferred and includes writer edits (p. 4, Section 2.2). These are output-pair exclusions, not 708 excluded people. The number of distinct writers remaining for each restricted outcome is not stated.
participants.who: Adults aged 18+ recruited on Prolific in the UK. The analyzed writer study sample is reported as 1,501 completers; writers were sampled to match UK census age, gender, and race. An additional 10,017 readers rated the writing; those raters are not added to the writer sample size (p. 11, Section 4.1).
participants.quote: Study 1 was completed by 1,501 writers and 10,017 readers

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o)
ai_tool.how_used: Structured drafting from the writer's stance rating or bullet points, or rewriting/improving the writer's own paragraph, followed by writer editing. Model/input pairings are randomized within writers in Studies 1 and 2. This is human use and editing of AI assistance, not an AI-only versus human-only output comparison. Models are accessed through OpenRouter (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.3-4.5).

task.description: Write political opinion paragraphs on three propositions sampled from a pool of 100. Writers first give a 0-100 stance rating, at least two explanatory bullet points, and their own paragraph of at least 100 words; they then edit an AI-generated paragraph until it reflects their opinion. AI paragraphs based on stance/bullets are requested at 100-150 words; paragraph-input conditions rewrite or improve the existing paragraph without changing its length (pp. 3, 11-12, Sections 2, 4.2, 4.4-4.5).

outcomes.name: Dispersion of perceived writer confidence across paragraphs
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The main text gives confidence as its numeric example of homogenization, reporting separate SDs for human-written and AI-assisted paragraphs. The observational and resampling units and any aggregation of ratings by paragraph or writer are not specified. These are dispersion outcomes, not the SDs for a creativity mean-difference effect. No confidence-specific uncertainty is printed (p. 4, Section 2.2; SI:5.9 referenced).

contrasts.reported: Perceived writer confidence: human-written paragraphs 24.1 SD versus AI-assisted paragraphs 20.5 SD. No attribute-specific p-value, CI, SE, or final analysis count is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.2, paragraph beginning "AI writing assistance also homogenised perceived writer personas"; details referred to SI:5.9, not in this PDF.

diversity_detail.metric: Standard deviation of perceived writer confidence ratings
diversity_detail.computed_over: Distributions of perceptions of human-written versus AI-assisted paragraphs across writers. The main text does not state whether ratings were first aggregated by paragraph or writer; the implementation is in unavailable SI:5.9 (p. 4, Section 2.2).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The main text reports significant SD/entropy reductions for 22 of 29 attributes at p<.001 after Bonferroni correction. Attribute-specific tests, SEs/CIs, resampling method, and the independent unit used for uncertainty are not supplied in this PDF; see SI:5.9 (p. 4, Section 2.2).
diversity_detail.notes: Lower dispersion means less diversity. This is dispersion of reader perceptions elicited by writing, not embedding similarity or lexical overlap. The analysis unit is null because the saved PDF does not specify the observational or resampling unit, or whether ratings were aggregated by paragraph or writer. A distributional summary alone does not establish unit=set under codebook Section 6. SI:5.9 is needed to identify the analysis unit (p. 4, Section 2.2).

outcomes.name: Perceived paragraph originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded lay readers rate the paragraph on a 0-100 scale. Average marginal effects are from beta regressions, on the original rating scale, with reader random effects only; writer and proposition effects were omitted because of convergence problems. Unit is an individual reader rating, not a writer mean. The exact number of ratings in each fitted analysis is not stated. The full paragraph pool includes edited and unedited AI versions and is not the final analysis count. Robustness analyses excluding edits and model/input variants are referred to SI:5.6-5.8, absent here (pp. 5, 12-13, Figure 2 and Sections 4.6-4.7). Originality is explicitly shown in Figure 2B, although omitted from the markdown image conversion; no exact question wording is printed outside SI:2.4.

contrasts.reported: +12.5 pts more original for AI-assisted versus human writing; *** denotes p<.001 after Bonferroni correction across all 29 attributes. AME on the original 0-100 scale; no numeric SE, CI, arm means, or arm SDs for this outcome are printed.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Disclaimer content was randomized between writers: acceptable distortions, unacceptable distortions, both, or no disclaimer. All writers used AI; this was not randomized AI availability. Models/input formats were varied within writers as in Study 1. Disclaimer order within a message was also randomized (p. 13, Section 4.9).
assignment.quote: The content of the disclaimer was randomly assigned at the writer level across three disclaimer conditions and a no-disclaimer control.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/sf7rg (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: No disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance without the pop-up disclaimer; control count is not printed in the saved PDF and is not obtained by subtraction (p. 13, Section 4.9).

arms.name: Acceptable-distortions disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus warning about clearer and more relevant writing. Printed N=160 is recorded as an analyzed writer count in the reported completed sample, not an initial randomized count (p. 13, Section 4.9; p. 11, Section 4.1).

arms.name: Unacceptable-distortions disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus warning about more extreme views and less openness to change (p. 13, Section 4.9).

arms.name: Both-types disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus all four distortion warnings (p. 13, Section 4.9).

participants.exclusions: Analyzed study sample: 669 writers, reported as study completers. Initial randomized counts and exclusions are not stated in this PDF; SI:1.4 is cited for attrition information (p. 11, Section 4.1; p. 13, Section 4.9).
participants.who: UK adults on Prolific; new writer sample, targeted census representativeness as in Study 1. No third-party rating panel was collected for this study (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.1 and 4.6).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o)
ai_tool.how_used: Structured drafting from the writer's stance rating or bullet points, or rewriting/improving the writer's own paragraph, followed by writer editing. Model/input pairings are randomized within writers in Studies 1 and 2. This is human use and editing of AI assistance, not an AI-only versus human-only output comparison. Models are accessed through OpenRouter (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.3-4.5).

task.description: Write political opinion paragraphs on three propositions sampled from a pool of 100. Writers first give a 0-100 stance rating, at least two explanatory bullet points, and their own paragraph of at least 100 words; they then edit an AI-generated paragraph until it reflects their opinion. AI paragraphs based on stance/bullets are requested at 100-150 words; paragraph-input conditions rewrite or improve the existing paragraph without changing its length (pp. 3, 11-12, Sections 2, 4.2, 4.4-4.5). Study 2 did not collect third-party ratings of originality or quality; its outcomes concern writer editing and preference (p. 12, Section 4.6; p. 13, Section 4.9).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each writer experienced Prompting, Reranking, and No Intervention across their three propositions in random order. This supports a randomized within-person ai_design comparison. The writer's own unaided paragraph remains a preceding reference, not a randomized no-AI arm (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).
assignment.quote: Assignment was such that each writer, across the three propositions they were assigned, experienced all three conditions in random order, in a within-subjects design.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/sf7rg (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: No Intervention
arms.description: Default AI paragraph generation from writer bullet points; every writer experiences this and both mitigation configurations. No separately stated final arm-level writer count (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).

arms.name: Prompting
arms.description: The AI generation prompt adds a 113-word instruction asking the model to preserve writer stance (p. 14, Section 4.10).

arms.name: Reranking
arms.description: The assigned AI model generates two sets of five candidate paragraphs; reward models select the candidate predicted to minimize stance discrepancy, with directional weighting against polarization (p. 14, Section 4.10).

arms.name: Own paragraph (unaided reference)
arms.description: Writer-produced paragraph before AI generation, used as a reference for distortion; this baseline is not one of the three randomized AI configurations (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).

participants.exclusions: Analyzed study sample: 769 writers, reported as study completers, not as an initial randomized total (p. 11, Section 4.1; p. 13, Section 4.10). Initial assignment, attrition, and outcome-specific distinct writer counts are unavailable in the main PDF; SI:1.4 is cited for attrition (p. 11). No condition-specific participant losses are reported; no zero-attrition assumption is made.
participants.who: New sample of UK adult writers recruited through Prolific with census-representative targets. A separate panel of 2,543 readers rated the paragraphs; 1,469 of those readers also took part in Study 1. Readers are not counted as writers assigned writing assistance (p. 11, Section 4.1).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o); GPT-4.1-based fine-tuned reward models for Reranking
ai_tool.how_used: The system supplies a complete opinion paragraph generated from the writer's bullet points; the writer can edit that draft and choose it instead of their own paragraph. This is full-paragraph drafting followed by human revision. Prompting asks the model to preserve stance, and Reranking selects a candidate using two GPT-4.1-based reward models trained on Study 1 data (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4-4.5 and 4.10).

task.description: Political opinion writing as in Study 1, with three propositions per writer; AI generation uses bullet-point inputs only. After generating a paragraph under the assigned mitigation configuration, writers can edit it. Separate blinded readers score the same 29 attributes, including originality, clarity, informativeness, relevance, and formality (pp. 7, 12-14, Sections 2.5, 4.4, 4.6, 4.10; attribute labels p. 5, Figure 2B).

outcomes.name: Perceived paragraph originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 3 collected blinded ratings on the same 29 attributes as Study 1, including originality and writing quality. Models use an intervention-condition regressor and reader random effects; the analysis unit is a reader rating. The printed reductions describe changes in AI-induced distortion relative to human writing, not standardized creativity effects or absolute arm means. Precise model outputs and additional contrasts are in unavailable SI:8.4. The paragraph pool of 5,016 is not a verified final per-outcome rating count (pp. 7, 12, 14, Sections 2.5, 4.6, 4.10). Originality is one of the writing-quality attributes shown in Figure 2B (p. 5). Study 3 rates the same attributes, but an identifiable originality effect, direction, SE, or CI for Reranking/Prompting versus No Intervention is not supplied in the main PDF. No direction is inferred from unlabeled points in Figure 4E.

studies.label: Study 4: Randomized reader exposure in a Trust Game

assignment.what_was_assigned: Readers saw one paragraph from each human/AI-assisted by low/high-distortion cell in random order. Assignment is to text exposure, not AI-assisted writing. Each cell had 200 stimulus paragraphs, not 200 participants.
assignment.quote: Paragraph assignment was such that each Study 4 reader was assigned one paragraph from each cell in random order in a within-subjects design, without ever being assigned more than one paragraph per proposition.

eligibility.reason: Study 3 meets all three criteria in the same study. Each writer experienced Prompting, Reranking and No Intervention in random within-person order (p. 13, Section 4.10). Its analyzed study sample is 769 writers, reported as completers, well above the people threshold; auxiliary readers are not added (p. 11, Section 4.1; p. 13, Section 4.10). Blinded readers scored participant-produced paragraphs on the same attributes as Study 1, including originality and writing quality (p. 5, Figure 2B; p. 12, Sections 4.5-4.6; p. 14, Section 4.10). Figure 4D reports Reranking-versus-No-Intervention attenuation of clarity, informativeness, relevance and formality distortions (p. 8); the unreported Study 3 originality estimate limits extraction, not confirmation that originality was scored. Study 1 supplies observational context for the recorded fixed-order AI-versus-unaided contrasts; its model/input randomization does not randomize that pooled comparison (p. 3, Figure 1; p. 12, Section 4.4). Study 2 has no third-party output ratings (p. 12, Section 4.6). Studies 4-5 randomize reader exposure to existing paragraphs, not AI assistance for new creative production (pp. 14-15, Sections 4.11-4.12). Unverified Study 1 dispersion units are now null. Missing supplement details, exact counts in restricted output analyses and writer-level uncertainty remain extraction or pooling gaps; none leaves an eligibility criterion unresolved. No after_ai creative task is reported.

one_line_finding: In the fixed-order comparison, AI-assisted paragraphs were rated +12.5 points more original (p. 5, Figure 2B) and showed lower dispersion on 22 of 29 attributes (p. 4, Section 2.2), while randomized reranking attenuated the AI-induced clarity increase by 26.9% (p. 8, Figure 4D).

notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading all 390 markdown lines, including references, and checking the saved PDF passages and the embedded Figures 2 and 4 in memory. The saved PDF has 20 pages, ends with references, and contains no appendix or embedded attachment. Repeated Python urllib requests to the named GitHub API, raw GitHub README and OSF API, with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no personal identifier, all failed with WinError 10013; no supplementary information was obtained. One challenge correction changes the five unverified dispersion units from set to null; the omitted-outcomes challenge is rejected under the current 15-outcome rule. All existing reported outcome numbers and contrast arrays are retained after PDF verification. Count prose now identifies analyzed study samples while preserving the source completer basis; unknown assignment totals and restricted-analysis counts remain null. All five prior open questions are assessed in final.open_items, with counts split into initial attrition and restricted-analysis counts. Reconciliation has no unresolved differences and its object is preserved unchanged. The following records the earlier reconciliation and retained coding rationale. Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both valid raw forms. Read all 390 markdown lines, including references; no appendix is included. Checked the PDF text on design, methods, sample and result pages; extracted tables on pp. 5 and 8 (none found) and inspected those embedded figure images in memory. Every retained outcome number was verified against its PDF page or printed figure label; no effect size, standard error, arm size, mean or unlabeled figure coordinate was calculated. GitHub API (api.github.com/repos/paul-rottger/ai-distortion/contents), raw GitHub README, and OSF API (api.osf.io/v2/nodes/sf7rg/) requests used Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1; all failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden). No supplementary content or preregistration was obtained. Difference counting aligns outcomes and arms by meaning, not array position or outcome_id. Equivalent wording, capitalization, compatible supplementary-section detail, /overview URL variants and empty synthesis placeholders are not substantive differences. Both forms contain the same 15 outcomes with the same construct, question, measure, analysis unit, AI availability, timing, primary status, directions and numerical estimates. The five statistics_available disagreements are retained as coding differences; their printed point estimates and locators agree. Coding decisions: Study 1 is quasi_people for the pooled contrasts actually recorded; its model/input randomization is documented separately. Its individual unit denotes the writer in the fixed-order comparison, not a claim of randomized AI access. Studies 4-5 are online_rct because reader exposure/order was randomized on Prolific; design class does not itself establish core eligibility. Their arms are coded ai=none because current participants receive existing reading stimuli, not assistance to produce writing; the description preserves each stimulus's AI authorship. Study 3 role=other describes complete-paragraph drafting followed by human editing; it does not describe open chat or delivery of ideation examples. The statistics_available label p_value_only describes the available inferential precision for numerically labeled AMEs and percentage attenuations without numerical SEs/CIs. The exact printed values and figure locations remain in reported and locator; figure_only is not needed to convey those already-transcribed numerical labels. Confidence dispersion retains an empty availability list because SDs alone match none of the supplied complete-statistic formats. The context_class=observational entry describes Study 1 and is compatible with core=yes through Study 3. Participant n_analyzed fields retain the paper's reported completed study samples: writers in Studies 1-3, behavioral reader subjects in Studies 4-5. These are not initial randomized totals. Distinct-writer counts in restricted outcome analyses remain unknown; none is imputed. Within-person arm Ns must not be summed. Separate rating panels are described but never added to the writer counts. Study 1 is explicitly the main study, with 1,501 writers; the qualifying randomized Study 3 has 769 writers (p. 11). Study 1 paragraph/rating pool totals of 10,008 and 2,903,596 (p. 3, Figure 1) and Study 3's 5,016 paragraphs (p. 12, Section 4.6) are not final per-outcome Ns, so n_units remains null. The 15-outcome cap retains the five writing attributes in each of Studies 1 and 3 plus Study 1 dispersion of confidence, originality, clarity, informativeness and relevance. The other 24 Study 1 attribute-specific dispersion analyses are not entered separately; the 22-of-29 family result is retained without assigning unreported individual effects. Changes in inferred writer traits/demographics, political extremity, preferences, tolerance, editing rates, model prediction error, reader trust and reader persuasion are not entered as creativity outcomes. Formality is coded other and is not interpreted as greater creativity. The common one-line finding was substantively identical in both raw forms; it is retained with explicit fixed-order versus randomized attribution. No after_ai creative task is reported: unaided writing came first, and later ratings concern already-produced text. Missing supplement-based estimates and counts are shared extraction gaps in open_questions, not unresolved A-versus-B disagreements.

differences.b: Political opinion writing: for each of 3 propositions sampled from 100, provide a 0-100 stance rating, at least 2 bullet-point reasons and an unaided paragraph of at least 100 words, then review and optionally edit an AI-generated paragraph. AI prompts request 100-150 words from stance/bullet inputs or rewriting/improvement without changing length from paragraph inputs (p. 3, Figure 1 and Results; p. 11, section 4.2; p. 12, sections 4.4-4.5). These are open-ended paragraphs assessed for originality and quality, not a divergent-thinking test.

open_items.item: Study 3 originality estimates, full configuration contrasts and numerical SEs/CIs remain unavailable; inspect SI:8.4 (p. 14, Section 4.10). This limits effect extraction, not criterion 3: the main paper already establishes output scoring.

Study 1 dispersion analysis unit, rating aggregation, repeated-output dependence, uncertainty methods and attribute-specific SD/entropy results, including omitted attributes, require SI:5.9 (p. 4, Section 2.2). These are contextual outcome-extraction gaps; Study 3 independently meets the output criterion.

Initial assignment totals and participant attrition require SI:1.4 (p. 11, Section 4.1). They do not leave criterion 2 unresolved: the reported analyzed Study 3 sample comprises 769 writers, with completer status explicit (pp. 11 and 13, Sections 4.1 and 4.10).

Exact distinct-writer counts by outcome and arm after output-based restrictions are not printed (p. 4, Section 2.2; pp. 12-14, Sections 4.6-4.10). Posted data linking included ratings and paragraphs to writer IDs would settle them. These counts are needed for extraction; the reported Study 3 study-level sample already establishes criterion 2.

Uncertainty suitable for pooling must respect writer-level assignment and repeated outputs; reader-perception regressions use reader random effects only (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.7 and 4.10). Reanalysis of posted data with writer-linked observations would settle this. It affects pooling, not any of the three screening criteria.

Study 1 randomized AI-model/input contrasts may be extractable from SI:5.7-5.8 (p. 13, Section 4.7). This could add eligible configuration contrasts but is not needed for criterion 1, already met by Study 3; the recorded pooled AI-versus-unaided comparison remains nonrandomized.
